label: 0A
title: First Steps: Values, Functions & Control Flow
summary: Variables, mutability and shadowing, number types, functions and return values, expressions vs statements, if/else and match as expressions (Rust's ternary), and loops.

quest.title: Learning the Ropes
quest.story:
You have just signed on with the **Crab Fleet** as the greenest deckhand aboard. Before anyone trusts you with the ledger (that comes in Level 1), the bosun wants to see that you can read and write the ship's language: Rust.

The ship's computer is run by an old parrot named *Rustc*. It reads every program before it runs and squawks at anything suspicious. It looks fussy, but every squawk is a bug that will never reach the open sea.

Your first watch is to learn how values are named and changed, how functions hand back answers, and how a Rust program makes decisions and repeats work. Pay special attention to one thing the bosun keeps repeating: **in Rust, almost everything is an expression and has a value.** That includes `if` and `match`, and it is why Rust doesn't need the `cond ? a : b` operator you may know from other languages.

Ring the ship's bells correctly at the end of this watch, and you're ready for strings.

concepts.title: Your first program: main, println! and format!
let, mut and shadowing
concepts.body:
`let` gives a value a name. Names are **immutable** by default:

```rust
let gold = 10;
gold = 12; // error[E0384]: cannot assign twice to immutable variable
```

Add `mut` when you really want to change a variable in place:

```rust
let mut gold = 10;
gold += 2;       // 12; also -=, *=, /=, %=
```

**Shadowing** is different: a second `let` with the same name creates a **new** variable that hides the old one. The new one can even have a different type:

```rust
let depth = "12";              // text
let depth = 12;                // a new variable, now a number
let depth = depth * 2;         // 24, still immutable
```

Use `mut` for a value that changes step by step (a counter, a running total). Use shadowing when you transform a value into the next stage and never need the old one again. You'll see `let log = add_line(log, …);` a lot in Level 1.

concepts.title: Number types, bool and char
concepts.body:
Every value has a type, and rustc usually infers it. You can always write it out: `let x: u32 = 5;`

- `i32`: signed integer, the default for integer literals (`-7`, `42`)
- `u32`, `u64`: unsigned, never negative (`7u32`)
- `i64`: a bigger signed integer (`0i64`)
- `usize`: sizes and indexes, e.g. what `.len()` returns
- `f64`: floating point (`2.5`)
- `bool`: `true` / `false`, e.g. `gold > 3`
- `char`: one Unicode character in **single** quotes (`'a'`, `'🦀'`)

Rust never converts number types silently. `let x: f64 = some_u32;` is error **E0308** (mismatched types). Convert explicitly:

```rust
let cups: u32 = 50;
let crew: u32 = 4;
let int_share = cups / crew;               // 12: integer division truncates
let rest = cups % crew;                    // 2: remainder
let share = cups as f64 / crew as f64;     // 12.5
let big = i64::from(cups);                 // lossless conversion
```

Integer overflow is a **panic** in the tutor's debug builds: `0u32 - 1` stops the program with "attempt to subtract with overflow". Use `a.saturating_sub(b)` when you want it to stop at 0. Other handy methods are `a.min(b)`, `a.max(b)`, `n.abs()` and `n.pow(2)`.

concepts.title: Functions and return values
Expressions vs statements
if is an expression: Rust's ternary
concepts.body:
Rust has **no** `cond ? a : b` operator. It doesn't need one, because `if`/`else` is itself an expression:

```rust
let rank = if gold > 50 { "captain" } else { "deckhand" };
let fee = if member { 0 } else { 5 } + base;
println!("{} bell{}", n, if n == 1 { "" } else { "s" });
```

The rules that make it work:

- Both branches must have the **same type**. `if c { 1 } else { "one" }` is E0308.
- When you use the value, the `else` is **required**. `let x = if c { 1 };` is error E0317, because there is no value when `c` is false.
- The condition must be a real `bool`. `if n { … }` with a number is E0308. Write `if n != 0`.
- `else if` chains work as you'd expect, and the whole chain is still one expression:

```rust
let wind = if speed == 0 { "calm" } else if speed < 20 { "breeze" } else { "gale" };
```

The braces are mandatory, and the condition needs no parentheses.

concepts.title: match as an expression
concepts.body:
`match` compares a value against **patterns** from top to bottom and evaluates the first arm that fits. Like `if`, it is an expression:

```rust
let mood = match gold % 10 {
    0 => "round",
    1 | 2 | 3 => "low",     // | means "or"
    4..=6 => "middling",    // inclusive range
    _ => "high",            // _ matches anything else
};
```

A `match` must be **exhaustive**: every possible value needs an arm. For numbers that almost always means a final `_` arm. Otherwise rustc stops with **E0004** (non-exhaustive patterns). All arms must have the same type. An arm can also be a block: `0 => { println!("empty"); 0 }`.

Prefer `match` over long `else if` chains when you compare **one** value against several constants or ranges. Level 3 shows its real power with enums.

concepts.title: Loops: loop, while and for

steps.note: main gets a stack frame. gold is an i32 that lives directly in it.
crew is declared mut, so it may change later.
crew += 1 changes the same slot in place. Only allowed because of mut.
Calling split pushes a new frame. The arguments are copied into total and n.
The body's last expression, total / n, is the return value. Integer division gives 10.
split's frame is gone. Its result became share.
if/else is an expression: 10 > 5, so the whole if is worth "rich".
Shadowing: a NEW gold (30) hides the old one. The old value is unreachable (faded) until main ends.
End of main: the whole frame is popped. Stack values need no cleanup.

challenges.title: Captain or deckhand?
challenges.story: The bosun sorts new hands by the gold in their purse, and his sorting program looks odd to you. Where is the `? :`?
challenges.prompt: Read the program. What does it print?
hints: Both `if` and `match` are expressions here: each one produces a value that goes straight into a `let`.
Is 42 greater than 50? And what is `42 % 10`, the remainder after dividing by 10?
`gold > 50` is false, so `rank` is `"deckhand"`. `42 % 10` is 2, which falls into `1..=4`.

choices.label: Compile error: `if` can't produce a value. You'd need `gold > 50 ? "captain" : "deckhand"`

challenges.title: One semicolon too many
challenges.story: The cook wrote a function to double the rum ration. *Rustc* squawks before the program even runs.
challenges.prompt: What happens when you compile and run this program?
hints: What is the value of a block whose last line ends with a semicolon?
`n * 2;` is a statement, so the body produces `()`. The signature promises an `i32`.
rustc rejects the mismatch at compile time: expected `i32`, found `()`. Removing the `;` fixes it.

choices.label: It prints `0`: the function falls off the end and returns the default
Compile error E0308: mismatched types, the body evaluates to `()`
It compiles, but panics when `double` returns nothing

challenges.title: Fix the ration sheet
challenges.story: The purser's ration program counts barrels and splits the rum between the crew. It doesn't compile, and *Rustc* has two complaints.
challenges.prompt:
Make the program compile and print exactly:

```text
5 barrels, 50 cups, 12.5 each
```

Rules:
- Keep `barrels`, `crew` and `cups` as integers and keep `crew: u32`.
- Compute `each` from `cups` and `crew` with an `as f64` conversion. Don't type `12.5` into the code.
- Don't change the `println!` line.
hints: There are two errors. Read each one: one is about changing a variable, the other is about types.
`barrels` is changed after it is created, so it must be declared `mut` (E0384). `cups / crew` is an integer division whose result is a `u32`, and `each` wants an `f64` (E0308).

`let mut barrels = 3;` and `let each: f64 = cups as f64 / crew as f64;`. Converting only the result (`(cups / crew) as f64`) would give `12.0`, because the integer division already threw away the `.5`.

require.message: Convert with `as f64`, as the rules say.

challenges.title: Tripling the catch
challenges.story: A fisherman's tally program: the catch triples every day until the hold is full, and then the log number is written backwards.
hints: Trace `n` by hand: 1, then 3, … When does `n >= 20` first hold? `break n` hands that value out of the `loop`.
`1..4` is 1, 2, 3 (the end is excluded), and `.rev()` walks it backwards.
`n` goes 1 → 3 → 9 → 27, and 27 is the first value ≥ 20. `log` goes 3 → 32 → 321.

challenges.title: Decisions at the helm
challenges.story: The helmsman needs three tiny functions for the instruments. The bosun's rule: no `return` keyword anywhere. Let `if` and `match` produce the values.
challenges.prompt:
Implement the three functions, using `if`/`else` and `match` **as expressions**. The keyword `return` is not allowed in this challenge.

- `fn larger(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32`: the larger of the two numbers.
- `fn sign(n: i32) -> i32`: `-1` for negative numbers, `0` for zero, `1` for positive numbers.
- `fn wind(knots: u32) -> &'static str`: `"calm"` for 0, `"breeze"` for 1 to 19, `"gale"` for 20 to 49, and `"storm"` for 50 and above.

`&'static str` is the type of text written in quotes in your program: it lives for the whole run. Just return literals like `"calm"`. Level 2 explains the `'static` part.

Hidden tests call all three functions directly.
hints: The value of a function is its last expression. If that last expression is an `if` or a `match`, its value is returned.
`sign` needs three branches: `if … { } else if … { } else { }`. For `wind`, `match` on `knots` with range patterns like `1..=19` and a final `_`.
`larger`: `if a > b { a } else { b }`. `wind`: `match knots { 0 => "calm", 1..=19 => "breeze", 20..=49 => "gale", _ => "storm" }`.

forbid.message: No `return` in this challenge: let the if/match expression be the function's last expression.

challenges.title: The navigator's riddle
challenges.story: The navigator passes the long night watches with an old riddle: take a number. If it's even, halve it. If it's odd, triple it and add one. Repeat until you reach 1. How many steps does it take?
challenges.prompt:
Write two functions:

- `fn steps_to_one(n: u64) -> u32`: how many steps the rule needs to bring `n` down to 1. The rule is: even → `n / 2`, odd → `3 * n + 1`. `steps_to_one(1)` is `0`, and `steps_to_one(6)` is `8` (6 → 3 → 10 → 5 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1). `n` is always at least 1.
- `fn longest_start(limit: u64) -> u64`: the starting number in `1..limit` (the limit itself excluded) that needs the **most** steps. On a tie, the smaller number wins. `limit` is always at least 2.

Keep a `fn main()`; it can print something or stay empty. Hidden tests call both functions. After they pass, the tutor judges whether your solution is idiomatic.
challenges.starter:
// Write steps_to_one(n: u64) -> u32 and longest_start(limit: u64) -> u64 here.

fn main() {}
hints: `steps_to_one` repeats until `n` is 1, so a `while n != 1` loop and a counter fit well. To change the parameter, declare it `mut n: u64`.
The next value is a choice between two expressions, which is exactly what `if … { } else { }` is for: `n = if n % 2 == 0 { … } else { … };`.

For `longest_start`, loop `for start in 1..limit`, and keep the best start and its step count in two `mut` variables. Update them only when the new count is strictly greater, so ties keep the smaller start.
challenges.rubric: Idiomatic, beginner-level Rust: a `while`/`loop` with the next value chosen by an `if`/`else` **expression** (e.g. `n = if n % 2 == 0 { n / 2 } else { 3 * n + 1 };`) or a `match` expression, a `mut` parameter or one local `mut` copy, and the result as the last expression without `return` at the end. `longest_start` uses a `for` loop over a range (or an iterator such as `max_by_key` with care for ties) and keeps ties on the smaller start. Deduct for recursion that can overflow the stack, needless `as` casts between integer types, magic numbers, or mutating more variables than needed. Do not deduct for using explicit loops instead of iterator adapters.

challenges.title: Boss: The Ship's Bells
challenges.story: At sea, time is kept by the **ship's bell**. It is struck every half hour: 1 bell at half past, 2 bells on the hour after, up to 8 bells at the end of each four-hour watch, and then it starts again. The old bell program was written by a sailor who missed the `? :` operator from another language, and it doesn't even compile.
challenges.prompt:
Fix and finish the bell program. Time is given as `minutes` after midnight, from 0 to 1439. Hidden tests call these four functions; keep their signatures:

- `fn bells(minutes: u32) -> u32`: only on a full or half hour (`minutes % 30 == 0`) is the bell struck, otherwise it's `0`. Count the half hours since midnight and keep the remainder after dividing by 8; a remainder of 0 means **8** bells. `00:30` → 1, `04:00` → 8, `04:30` → 1, `00:00` → 8, `00:10` → 0.
- `fn watch(minutes: u32) -> &'static str`: by the hour (`minutes / 60`): 0–3 `"middle"`, 4–7 `"morning"`, 8–11 `"forenoon"`, 12–15 `"afternoon"`, 16–17 `"first dog"`, 18–19 `"last dog"`, 20–23 `"first"`.
- `fn clock(minutes: u32) -> String`: `HH:MM` with leading zeros, e.g. `04:05`, `23:30`.
- `fn log_line(minutes: u32) -> String`: `"{clock} {watch} watch, {n} bell"` with `bells` instead of `bell` when n is not 1, and `"no bell"` when n is 0. Examples:

```text
04:30 morning watch, 1 bell
12:00 afternoon watch, 8 bells
16:10 first dog watch, no bell
```

There is no `?:` in Rust: use `if`/`else` expressions. `main` may print whatever you like.
hints: Fix the compile errors first, in the order rustc reports them. The very first one is a syntax error: Rust has no `? :` operator. What expression gives you "this value or that value"?
After that: an `if` used as a value needs an `else` (E0317); a `match` on a number needs a final `_` arm (E0004); and a function whose last line ends in `;` returns `()` (E0308).

Once it compiles, the tests check the details. `{:02}` pads a number to two digits with zeros. `bells` needs three cases: not on a half hour → 0, remainder 0 → 8, otherwise the remainder. `log_line` needs a third case for `"no bell"`.

`bells`: `if minutes % 30 != 0 { 0 } else if half_hours % 8 == 0 { 8 } else { half_hours % 8 }`. `log_line`: `let count = if n == 0 { String::from("no bell") } else { format!("{} bell{}", n, if n == 1 { "" } else { "s" }) };`.

cards.front: How do you write C's `cond ? a : b` in Rust?
cards.back: Rust has **no** `?:` operator. `if` is an expression, so write `if cond { a } else { b }`, e.g. `let rank = if gold > 50 { "captain" } else { "deckhand" };`. Both branches must have the same type, and the `else` is required when you use the value.

cards.front: What does `let mood = match n { 0 => "none", 1..=9 => "few", _ => "many" };` show about `match`?
cards.back: `match` is an **expression**: the chosen arm's value becomes `mood`. Patterns can be literals, `a | b`, ranges like `1..=9`, and `_` for everything else. A `match` must be exhaustive (otherwise E0004), and all arms must have the same type.

cards.front: Why does `fn double(n: i32) -> i32 { n * 2; }` fail to compile?
cards.back: The `;` turns `n * 2` into a **statement**, so the block evaluates to `()`. The signature promises `i32`: error **E0308** (mismatched types). Remove the semicolon: the last expression *without* `;` is the return value.

cards.front: `let x = 5; x += 1;`: what does rustc say, and what are the two ways forward?
cards.back: **E0384**: cannot assign twice to an immutable variable. Either declare it `let mut x = 5;` (change it in place), or **shadow** it: `let x = x + 1;` (a new variable with the same name).

cards.front: `cups: u32 = 50`, `crew: u32 = 4`. What are `cups / crew`, `cups % crew` and `cups as f64 / crew as f64`?
cards.back: `12` (integer division truncates), `2` (the remainder), and `12.5`. Rust never converts number types implicitly. Assigning a `u32` to an `f64` is E0308, so convert with `as` (or `f64::from`).

cards.front: How do you get a value out of a loop?
cards.back: With `loop` and `break value`: `let x = loop { …; if done { break n; } };`. Only `loop` can do this, because `while` and `for` may end without hitting a `break`.

cards.front: What do `0..3`, `1..=3` and `(1..=3).rev()` produce in a `for` loop?
cards.back: `0, 1, 2` (the end is excluded), `1, 2, 3` (`..=` includes the end), and `3, 2, 1`.

cards.front: Name three rules for `if` used as a value.
cards.back: 1. Both branches have the same type (otherwise E0308). 2. An `else` is required (otherwise E0317). 3. The condition must be a `bool`: Rust has no "truthy" numbers, so write `if n != 0`, not `if n`.

cards.front: What happens at runtime with `let x: u32 = 0; let y = x - 1;` in a debug build, and how do you stop at zero instead?
cards.back: It **panics** with "attempt to subtract with overflow". Use `x.saturating_sub(1)`, which gives 0. In release builds overflow wraps silently, so don't rely on either behaviour by accident.
